Senses.Explanation: To present in full is to bring the whole matter forward without leaving a remainder; the phrase appears in questions, answers, and appraisals of complete presentation. Literally, to raise or present in full. Yunmen Wenyan supplies the decisive contrast: seeing no single form is only half-presentation, and even then one must know the occasion of full presentation . Shengyin Chongkai pairs presentation across past and present with the ancestral master's true command . Juelang Dasheng joins the flower at Vulture Peak and snow at Shaoshi with separate transmission personally shown and the true command fully presented . Yuanwu Keqin raises the command in full and publicly asks how it can be unfolded. Liao'an Qingyu says that the entrustment at Vulture Peak is precisely here and tells the assembly to take up one fully presented saying ; Shending Yunwai Ze similarly says that if one can present it whole with bare hands, ease is assured . Zen bends the ordinary sense of completeness toward teaching-seat language: a saying, command, or lineage entrustment is brought forward without remainder and submitted to the assembly.

AlternateTargets: bring forth the command in full

Senses.Note: The sole construction with the nominalizing person-marker (者) describes a person who broadly displayed the whole dynamic; it does not define a second sense. In Shiguan Fazang's autobiographical record, his teacher Juelang Daosheng asks ‘what is the whole dynamic?’ (如何是全機), and Shiguan answers by raising one finger; when asked about the whole function, he spreads both hands. The former entry incorrectly attached an unrelated ‘midnight sun’ answer to this exchange; exact KWIC review removes that error. The same referent spans direct discourse, case rubrics, verse, and prose comment, so neither grammatical variation nor different speakers warrant a second sense.

Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shiguan (石關禪師語錄): Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shiguan (石關禪師語錄), Shiguan Fazang's autobiographical account: his teacher Juelang Daosheng asks what the whole dynamic is and what the whole function is; Shiguan answers by raising one finger and then spreading both hands.

Senses.Explanation: The whole dynamic or full pivotal function: the complete working of a trigger or pivot. The graphs join ‘whole or complete’ (全) to ‘trigger, pivot, or dynamic’ (機). The compound has 948 occurrences in 244 texts. It is especially visible in ‘the whole dynamic and great function’ (全機大用). Yuanwu Keqin says this ‘whole dynamic and great function is manifest wherever one touches’ (全機大用觸處見成); elsewhere his record says ‘as the grass bends and the wind moves, the whole dynamic alone is exposed’ (草偃風行全機獨露), then asks what one says without relying on any thing or phrase. Yuanwu also speaks of the whole dynamic ‘alone functioning’ (全機獨用). Chaozong Tongren pairs a wisdom-sword cutting bonds with the whole dynamic ‘thoroughly freed’ (全機透脫), then immediately glosses being freed as a sick person finally sweating. The Blue Cliff Record uses the term both in Yuanwu's case pointer ‘the whole dynamic is displayed everywhere’ (全機隨處齊彰) and in his comment that several actions are all ‘places of the whole dynamic and great function’ (全機大用處). Gongchen Daoxian uses the compound predicatively: ‘if I deploy the whole dynamic, where will you search?’ (我若全機，汝向甚麼處摸索). The records thus bend an ordinary word for the complete working of a mechanism into language for undivided operation at the teaching seat.

Senses.Explanation: The whole body stands exposed means that the complete thing is already openly displayed, even where the person facing it fails to recognize it. Wuwai Wunian Yuanxin gives the contrast in one exchange: face-to-face it is not recognized, yet its whole body stands openly exposed. Miyun Wuyun likewise places the phrase in broad daylight under a clear sky after refusing both talk and silence as resting places. The exposed whole is not restricted to a human body. Ruibai Mingxue uses one jewel whose full body is present through its colored reflections; Puan Yinsu uses one broken grain of ordinary Luling rice; Jifei Ruyi answers from within the ocean-seal’s light. These images make exposure observable through what is present rather than through a hidden explanation. Failure to recognize it and differences among reflected colors do not make the whole absent. Body, jewel, grain, and luminous field are distinct images carrying one recurrent predicate: the complete referent is out in the open. They are not four separate dictionary senses.

Senses.Explanation: A token of trust is an object presented or retained as evidence of acknowledgment or transmission, especially a robe, staff, or whisk. Feiyin Tongrong raises the robe and asks how trust can be shown after saying masters use it as a token. Miyun Yuanwu says the ancestral robe was transmitted as such a token and contrasts it with his own present verification. The Huineng-Huiming case calls the robe a token not worth fighting over. Later instructions entrust a whisk or staff to a student as a token to be kept and eventually brought out.
